I love Vietnamese coffee, but had no idea how to make it so it tasted right. Thus, Vietnamese coffee was reserved for a special treat when I went to my local coffee shop. The barista recommended that I buy a filter. Best advice ever. Now that I have purchased this Vietnamese coffee filter, I can treat myself at home any time.

Vietnamese coffee uses a coarsely ground, dark roast coffee (Robusta beans, not Arabica) and sweetened condensed milk to make a smooth, creamy, kinda-chocolately-but-still-coffee-flavored concoction that is like heaven in a cup. You can drink hot (so decadent) or over ice (so refreshing).

The process of brewing Vietnamese coffee is time consuming, but the philosophy is that the brewing and enjoyment is part of the whole experience. That said, sometimes I just don't have the time to enjoy the brewing process. I have started to brew individual cups into small (8oz) mason jelly jars to keep in my fridge. Now if I am in a hurry and want a quick iced coffee, I can just grab a jar and pour over ice on my way out the door.

This coffee maker relies on a slow drip, about 4-5 minutes. I heat water up to boiling point. Then grind the beans at a medium grind , put base filter in pot, pour coffee over this filter and try to get the grinds level in the pot. A small tamper would work here. I am still working on this. Then screw the top filter on to stem of bottom filter. But not too tight or water may not get through. Try screwing down the top filter just enough to touch the grounds. Then pour in at least one cup of hot water. Back up: The pot needs to sit on top  of  coffee mug or glass, then pour water over it. Cover while dripping to save flavor. You can add milk before or after water is added, if you use it. This procedures is WELL worth the wait, because the flavor does not have the sharp bite that high pressure espresso machines can create. The result is strong but mellow! And that IS incredible!  Ed

I absolutely love my ice maker!  I have worked it pretty hard over the last year.  In fact, my sister loves it so much that I purchased one for her birthday.  We live in the country where even with a water softener it doesn't get all the minerals out of the water.  So, I use gallon jugs of drinking water and refill them at the store.  Each time I make ice it uses around a half gallon of water.  Of course, depending on the size of cubes you make there may be differences in the amount of ice that is made.  For me, I use the largest cubes and  have about 3 gallon bags of ice.  (I would freeze the ice after making it.  It will stick together, so you may want to check it periodically; or, you can break it loose later.  Personally, I use the back of an ice cream scoop and break the ice loose).  One of my favorite things about this ice maker is that the ice is a softer consistency.  It crushes easily for smoothies, margaritas.  It's soft enough for kids with sore throats or just adding juice for a cool summer drink.  If you love eating ice; this ice maker is for you! .
